newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear accident is bad news for power plans.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear accident is bad news for power plans.

text.p: Japan's most serious atomic energy accident could not have come in a worse week for the country's nuclear power industry.

The incident, in which a radiation leak contaminated 35 workers, was just one blow in what could turn into more than a bad luck week for an industry regarded as a cornerstone of energy-starved Japan's economic policy.

Hours before the fire in a nuclear reprocessing plant at Tokaimura, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, the industry had already suffered a setback when local opposition elsewhere in Japan forced the scrapping of a planned nuclear power plant.
And on the horizon next Tuesday, environmental groups including Greenpeace plan protests against the arrival in a Japanese port of a ship carrying Japanese nuclear waste reprocessed in France.

The three events throw an unwelcome spotlight on nuclear energy in a country that both relies on it for one-third of its electricity needs and is uniquely aware of the dangers as a result of Japan's position as the only nation to have suffered atomic bombing.
With an eye on the three events, Citizens Nuclear Information Centre Secretary-General Hideyuki Ban said he expected the accident to have a significant psychological impact on the public.
"I think the (accident) is going to provide momentum to people calling for an end to Japan's plutonium energy policy," he said.

That is bad news for economic planners because Japan hopes plutonium technology will allow it to wean itself off oil imports to the point where by the early 21st century it will be able to supply more than half of its energy needs.

Nuclear planners were already reeling from the impact of a December 1995 accident and cover-up attempt at Monju, a prototype plutonium fast-breeder reactor, which was the centrepiece of the plutonium strategy.

Although no radiation leaked in the accident at Monju, the incident became a public relations disaster when the media revealed that the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation (PNC), owner of both the Monju and the Tokaimura plants, tried to keep videotapes of a coolant accident secret.
The shame and perception of betrayal of the public trust was so great that a PNC official at Monju committed suicide.
PNC chairman Yoshiyuki Kondo indicated how much the nuclear industry relied on public acceptance when, in his first comments on Tuesday's accident, he said:
"Tokaimura is the place where nuclear power in Japan was born and we have had the understanding of residents for a long time, and I deeply regret that this incident betrayed their trust.

"That radiation leaked -- even a little bit -- and that it affected human beings is a serious matter. Something that should have been avoided at all costs unfortunately occurred and we deeply regret it," he told reporters.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto gave his nod to the acceptance of the importance of public support when he profusely apologised in parliament for the hours-long delay in announcing details of the accident.

Manabu Hattori, a retired professor of nuclear science at Tokyo's Rikkyo University and a supporter of nuclear power, said the atomic energy industry and government needed to do more if it wanted to public support for energy policies.
"Not only the accident itself, but also the reaction of PNC disappointed people. I can't help saying the PNC and government haven't taken enough measures to handle such a situation," he told Reuters.
"I don't reject nuclear power itself as an energy resource, but there remain a lot of problem areas regarding its use. Japan has been rushing to use it while neglecting safety research."
